es.summary: Alteración del pH sanguíneo que refleja un exceso de ácido o base y compromete la función celular.
key_points: pH normal: 7.35‑7.45; valores fuera de este rango indican acidosis (<7.35) o alcalosis (>7.45).
Los pulmones regulan PaCO₂; los riñones regulan HCO₃⁻.
Compensación respiratoria o renal puede ser parcial o completa.
Los desequilibrios pueden ser metabólicos o respiratorios, simples o combinados.

pathophysiology: Aumento de ácidos o pérdida de bases disminuye el pH (acidosis).
Disminución de ácidos o exceso de bases eleva el pH (alcalosis).
Los pulmones ajustan la ventilación para eliminar CO₂ (ácido volátil).
Los riñones modifican la reabsorción y excreción de HCO₃⁻ y iones H⁺.
risk_factors: Enfermedad pulmonar obstructiva crónica (EPOC) o insuficiencia respiratoria.
Insuficiencia renal, diarrea profusa o vómitos prolongados.
Uso de diuréticos, laxantes o antiácidos en exceso.
Hipoperfusión tisular por shock o sepsis.
signs_symptoms: Alteración del nivel de conciencia, confusión o somnolencia.
Respiración rápida y profunda (Kussmaul) o hipoventilación.
Dolor de cabeza, náuseas y vómitos.
diagnostics: Gasometría arterial: pH, PaCO₂ (mmHg) y HCO₃⁻ (mEq/L).
Electrolitos séricos: Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, Ca²⁺ (mEq/L).
Análisis de lactato y glucosa (mg/dL) si se sospecha sepsis o hipoglucemia.
Radiografía de tórax y espirometría si se sospecha causa respiratoria.
treatment: Corrección de la causa subyacente (ej. antibiótico para infección, broncodilatador).
Ventilación mecánica o soporte de oxígeno para alteraciones respiratorias.
Reposición de bicarbonato sódico IV en acidosis metabólica grave.
Ajuste de diuréticos o fluidos IV según balance de volumen y electrolitos.
complications: Arritmias cardíacas por alteraciones de K⁺ y Ca²⁺.
nursing_care: Monitorear pH, PaCO₂ y HCO₃⁻ cada 2‑4 h según orden médica.
Evaluar patrón respiratorio, frecuencia y esfuerzo.
Controlar signos vitales, especialmente presión arterial y frecuencia cardíaca.
Registrar ingesta y pérdida de líquidos; vigilar balance de electrolitos.
Mantener vía aérea permeable y posicionar al paciente en semi‑Fowler.
patient_teaching: Explicar la importancia de la adherencia al tratamiento y al control de enfermedades crónicas.
Enseñar técnicas de respiración profunda y uso correcto del inhalador si corresponde.
Instruir sobre la ingesta adecuada de líquidos y alimentos ricos en electrolitos.
Alertar sobre signos de alarma: mareos, palpitaciones, dificultad para respirar.

outcomes: NOC: Equilibrio electrolítico – mantener Na⁺ 135‑145 mEq/L y K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L en 24 h.
NOC: Estado de hidratación – balance hídrico neto dentro de ±500 mL en 48 h.

interventions.action: Monitorear electrolitos séricos cada 4‑6 h y registrar valores.
interventions.rationale: Detectar desviaciones tempranas permite intervención oportuna.

interventions.action: Evaluar signos de deshidratación o sobrecarga (turgencia cutánea, edema).
interventions.rationale: Los cambios físicos reflejan alteraciones de volumen y electrolitos.

interventions.action: Administrar fluidos IV según prescripción, ajustando solución (ej. NaCl 0.9% o Ringer lactato).
interventions.rationale: Reemplaza pérdidas y corrige desequilibrios iónicos.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre dieta equilibrada en sodio y potasio.
interventions.rationale: La ingesta dietética ayuda a mantener niveles electrolíticos estables.

en.summary: Alteration of blood pH reflecting an excess of acid or base that compromises cellular function.
key_points: Normal pH: 7.35‑7.45; values outside this range indicate acidosis (<7.35) or alkalosis (>7.45).
Lungs regulate PaCO₂; kidneys regulate HCO₃⁻.
Respiratory or renal compensation may be partial or complete.
Imbalances can be metabolic or respiratory, simple or combined.

pathophysiology: Increase in acids or loss of bases decreases pH (acidosis).
Decrease in acids or excess of bases raises pH (alkalosis).
Lungs adjust ventilation to eliminate CO₂ (volatile acid).
Kidneys modify reabsorption and excretion of HCO₃⁻ and H⁺ ions.
risk_factors: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or respiratory failure.
Renal failure, profuse diarrhea or prolonged vomiting.
Excess use of diuretics, laxatives or antacids.
Tissue hypoperfusion from shock or sepsis.
signs_symptoms: Altered level of consciousness, confusion or drowsiness.
diagnostics: Arterial blood gas: pH, PaCO₂ (mmHg) and HCO₃⁻ (mEq/L).
Serum electrolytes: Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, Ca²⁺ (mEq/L).
Lactate and glucose analysis (mg/dL) if sepsis or hypoglycemia suspected.
Chest X‑ray and spirometry if respiratory cause suspected.
treatment: Correct underlying cause (e.g., antibiotic for infection, bronchodilator).
Mechanical ventilation or oxygen support for respiratory disturbances.
IV sodium bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidosis.
Adjust diuretics or IV fluids based on volume balance and electrolytes.
complications: Cardiac arrhythmias from K⁺ and Ca²⁺ disturbances.
nursing_care: Monitor pH, PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ every 2‑4 h per order.
Assess respiratory pattern, rate and effort.
Check vital signs, especially blood pressure and heart rate.
Record intake and output; monitor electrolyte balance.
Maintain airway patency and position patient in semi‑Fowler.
patient_teaching: Explain importance of adherence to treatment and chronic disease control.
Teach deep breathing techniques and correct inhaler use if applicable.
Instruct on adequate fluid intake and foods rich in electrolytes.
Alert to warning signs: dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath.

outcomes: NOC: Electrolyte Balance – maintain Na⁺ 135‑145 mEq/L and K⁺ 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L within 24 h.
NOC: Hydration Status – net fluid balance within ±500 mL in 48 h.

interventions.action: Monitor serum electrolytes every 4‑6 h and record values.
interventions.rationale: Early detection of deviations allows timely intervention.

interventions.action: Assess for signs of dehydration or overload (skin turgor, edema).
interventions.rationale: Physical changes reflect volume and electrolyte alterations.

interventions.action: Administer IV fluids per prescription, adjusting solution (e.g., 0.9% NaCl or lactated Ringer's).
interventions.rationale: Replaces losses and corrects ionic imbalances.

interventions.action: Educate patient on balanced diet in sodium and potassium.
interventions.rationale: Dietary intake helps maintain stable electrolyte levels.

summary.0.quote: Many enzymes and cellular processes do not function normally if the blood’s level of acid or base is too high or too low.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: Additionally, any fluid loss from the stomach level and above results in loss of acids and eventual alkalosis, whereas fluid losses below the stomach result in loss of bases and eventual acidosis.

sections.pathophysiology.2.quote: Nurses may first suspect that a patient has metabolic acidosis because the patient has rapid breathing; this occurs as the lungs try to remove excess CO 2 to resolve the acidosis.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: Under normal conditions, the kidneys work to maintain a normal pH by excreting acids through urine; they also neutralize excess acids by increasing bicarbonate (HCO 3 − ) reabsorption from the urine.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: Respiratory acidosis is typically caused by a medical condition such as an acute asthma exacerbation, COPD, or an acute heart failure exacerbation causing pulmonary edema ; these conditions all decrease the exchange of oxygen and CO 2 at the alveolar level .

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: For example, prolonged vomiting can result in alkalosis and prolonged diarrhea can result in acidosis.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: For example, loop and thiazide diuretics can create a secondary hyperaldosteronism that leads to excess urine excretion of hydrogen.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: Other signs and symptoms of metabolic acidosis include confusion decreased level of consciousness electrolyte disturbances that can progress to circulatory collapse and death if not treated promptly GI distress: diarrhea hyp

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: Nurses may first suspect that a patient has metabolic acidosis because the patient has rapid breathing; this occurs as the lungs try to remove excess CO 2 to resolve the acidosis.

sections.diagnostics.0.quote: Arterial blood gases are indicators of several parameters that can affect the body’s acid-base balance: the pH level of the blood, the partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO 2 ), the partial pressure of arterial carbon dioxide (PaCO 2 ), the bicarbonate level (HCO 3 − ), and the oxygen saturation level (SaO 2 ).

sections.treatment.0.quote: Once a probable cause of a patient’s metabolic acidosis has been identified, appropriate steps can be taken to correct the underlying problem (Burger & Schaller, 2023).

sections.treatment.1.quote: If these noninvasive interventions are not successful, the patient will likely need to be intubated and receive mechanical ventilation support.

sections.patient_teaching.2.quote: You get these electrolytes from the foods you eat and the fluids you drink.

sections.patient_teaching.3.quote: Patients experiencing respiratory alkalosis often report feelings of shortness of breath, dizziness or light-headedness, chest pain or tightness, paresthesia, and palpitations.
